items.title: clingo
items.text: Module providing functions and classes to control the grounding and solving process of Answer Set Programming (ASP).

items.title: Introduction
items.text: This module offers a comprehensive set of tools for interacting with the clingo ASP solver, allowing users to control grounding and solving processes programmatically.

items.title: Terms
items.text: Terms without variables and interpreted functions are called symbols in the following. They are wrapped in the Symbol class.

items.title: Symbolic Atoms and Literals
items.text: Symbolic atoms without variables and interpreted functions, which appear in ground logic programs, are captured using the Symbol class. They must be of type Function. Furthermore, some functions accept symbolic literals, which are represented as pairs of symbols and Booleans. The Boolean stands for the sign of the literal (True for positive and False for negative).

items.title: Program Literals
items.text: When passing a ground logic program to a solver, clingo does not use a human readable textual representation but the aspif format. The literals in this format are called program literals. They are non-zero integers associated with symbolic atoms, theory atoms, and also without any association if they are used to translate complex language constructs not directly representable in aspif format. The sign of a program literal is used to represent default negation. Symbolic and theory atoms can be mapped to program literals using the base module. Note that symbolic and theory atoms can share the same program literals. Finally, the backend module can also be used to introduce fresh symbolic atoms and program literals.

items.title: Solver Literals
items.text: Before solving, programs in aspif format are translated to an internal solver representation, where program literals are again mapped to non-zero integers, so called solver literals. The solver_literal function can be used to map program literals to solver literals. Note that different program literals can share the same solver literal.

items.title: Embedded Python Code
items.text: If the clingo application is built with Python support, clingo will also be able to execute Python code embedded in logic programs. Functions defined in a Python script block are callable during the instantiation process using @-syntax. The default grounding/solving process can be customized if a main function is provided.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The first example shows how to use Python code from clingo:

#script (python)

from typing import Sequence
from clingo.core import Library
from clingo.control import Control
from clingo.symbol import Number, Symbol

Parts = Sequence[Sequence[tuple[str, Sequence[Symbol]]]]

def f(lib: Library, x: Symbol):
    return Number(lib, x.number)

def main(lib: Library, ctl: Control, parts: Parts):
    for part in parts:
        ctl.ground(part)
        ctl.solve()

#end.

1 {p(1..2)} 1.
q(@f(X)) :- p(X).

The second example shows how to use the clingo module from Python. Note the use of a context object here. In fact, it is not possible (by default) to call functions from the main scope. See the script module for more information.

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>> from clingo.symbol import Number, Symbol
...
>>> class Context:
...     def __init__(self, lib: Library) -> None:
...         self.lib = lib
...     def f(self, x: Symbol):
...         return Number(self.lib, x.number + 1)
...
>>> with Library() as lib:
...     ctl = Control(lib, ["0"])
...     ctl.parse_string("1 {p(1..2)} 1. q(@f(X)) :- p(X).")
...     ctl.ground(context=Context(lib))
...     ctl.solve(on_model=print)

items.title: clingo.app
items.text:
Module to create custom clingo-based applications.

This module provides application-level functionality for working with clingo, including an application class, options definitions, and helper routines.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The following example shows how to run clingo without customization:

import sys
from clingo.app import clingo_main
from clingo.core import Library
from clingo.script import enable_python

with Library() as lib:
    enable_python(lib)
    clingo_main(lib, sys.argv[1:])

The next example shows how to write a simple clingo-based application that adds an option to print atoms in models in order:

from typing import Callable, Sequence
import sys
from clingo.app import App, AppOptions, Flag, clingo_main
from clingo.core import Library
from clingo.control import Control
from clingo.solve import Model

class MyApp(App):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__("my-app", "1.0.0")
        self._order = Flag()

    def print_model(self, model: Model, default_printer: Callable[[], None]) -> None:
        if self._order.value:
            print(" ".join(str(sym) for sym in sorted(model.symbols(shown=True))))
        else:
            default_printer()

    def register_options(self, options: AppOptions) -> None:
        options.add_flag(
            "MyApp", "order", "Print atoms in models in order.", self._order
        )

    def main(self, control: Control, files: Sequence[str]) -> None:
        control.parse_files(files)
        control.main()

with Library() as lib:
    sys.exit(clingo_main(lib, sys.argv[1:], MyApp()))

items.title: clingo.backend
items.text: Functions and classes to observe or add ground statements.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The first example shows how to add a fact to a program:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.symbol import Function
>>> from clingo.control import Control
...
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib)
>>> sym = Function(lib, "a")
>>> with ctl.backend as bck:
...     atm_a = bck.atom(sym)
...     bck.rule([atm_a])
>>> ctl.base.is_fact(ctl.base[sym].literal)
True
>>> print(ctl.solve(on_model=print))
a
SAT

The next example shows how to add theory atoms to a program: 

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.symbol import Function
>>> from clingo.control import Control
...
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib)
...
>>> with ctl.backend as bck:
...     n = Function(lib, "p")
...     a = bck.theory_string("a")
...     o = bck.theory_number(1)
...     f = bck.theory_function("f", [a, o])
...     e = bck.theory_element([f], [])
...     bck.theory_atom(0, n, [e])
...
>>> print(ctl.base.theory[0])
&p { f(a,1) }

items.title: clingo.base
items.text: Functions and classes to work with atom and term bases.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.symbol import Function, Number
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib)
>>> ctl.parse_string("""\
... p(1).
... { p(3) }.
... #external p(1..3).
...
... q(X) :- p(X).
... """)
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> bse = ctl.base
>>> len(bse)
2
>>> p = bse[("p", 1)]
>>> Function(lib, "p", [Number(lib, 2)]) in p
True
>>> Function(lib, "p", [Number(lib, 4)]) in p
False
>>> [sig for sig in bse]
[('p', 1, False), ('q', 1, False)]
>>> [(str(x.symbol), bse.is_fact(x.literal), bse.is_external(x.literal))
...  for x in p.values()]
[('p(1)', True, False), ('p(3)', False, False), ('p(2)', False, True)]

items.title: clingo.config
items.text: Functions and classes related to configuration.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The following example shows how inspect the configuration and modify it to enumerate all models:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib)
>>> ctl.config.attributes
['tester', 'solve', 'asp', 'solver', 'configuration', 'share',
 'learn_explicit', 'sat_prepro', 'stats', 'parse_ext', 'parse_maxsat']
>>> ctl.config.solve.attributes
['solve_limit', 'parallel_mode', 'global_restarts', 'distribute',
 'integrate', 'enum_mode', 'project', 'models', 'opt_mode', 'opt_stop']
>>> str(ctl.config.solve)
"""\
solve_limit: "umax,umax"
parallel_mode: "1,compete"
global_restarts: "no"
distribute: "no,conflict,global,4,4194303"
integrate: "gp,1024,all"
enum_mode: "auto"
project: "no"
models: "-1"
opt_mode: "-1,opt"
opt_stop: "-1,opt,no"\
"""
>>> ctl.config.solve.models.description
"Compute at most <n> models (0 for all)"
>>> ctl.config.solve.models = 0
>>> ctl.parse_string("1 {a; b}.")
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> print(ctl.solve(on_model=print))
b
a
a b
SAT

The next example shows how to extend the configuration with a custom entry:

from clingo.core import Library
from clingo.control import Control


class CustomConfig:
    value: str | None
    array: list[str | None]

    def __init__(self):
        self.value = None
        self.array = []

    def set_val(self, value: str):
        self.value = value

    def get_val(self):
        return self.value

    def get_arr_len(self):
        return len(self.array)

    def set_arr_val(self, value, index=None):
        if index is None:
            index = 0
        while len(self.array) <= index:
            self.array.append(None)
        self.array[index] = value

    def get_arr_val(self, index=None):
        if index is None:
            index = 0
        return self.array[index]


lib = Library()
ctl = Control(lib)
cfg = ctl.config
ctm = CustomConfig()

cfg.add_entry("custom", "simple example config")
cfg.add_entry("custom.val", "value", ctm.get_val, ctm.set_val)
cfg.add_entry("custom.arr[]", "array", size=ctm.get_arr_len)
cfg.add_entry(
    "custom.arr[].val", "value in array", get=ctm.get_arr_val, set=ctm.set_arr_val
)

cfg.custom.val = "a"
cfg.custom.arr[0].val = "b"
cfg.custom.arr[1].val = "c"

print(cfg.custom)

Running the above code produces the following output: 

arr:
  - val: "b"
  - val: "c"
val: "a"

items.title: Config
items.text:
Allows for changing the configuration of the underlying solver.

Options are organized hierarchically. To get or change the value of an option (identified by is_value) use:

config.group.subgroup.option = "value"        # variant 1 (short)
config.group.subgroup.option.value = "value"  # variant 2
value = config.group.subgroup.option.value

There are also sequences of option groups (identified by is_sequence):

config.group.subgroup[0].option = "value1"
config.group.subgroup[1].option = "value2"

Use the attributes member to list subgroups of an option group. Meta options with key configuration set multiple related options when assigned. Use description for more information about an option or option group.

Notes:

  • The first element of a sequence can be accessed directly without index 0.
  • Config objects have a YAML-like string representation for inspection.
  • In string representations of sequences, attributes (for index 0) are only added if the sequence is empty.
  • Option values are always strings; assigned values are automatically converted to strings.

items.title: add_entry
items.text:
add_entry(
    name: str,
    description: str,
    get: ValueGetter | SequenceGetter | None = None,
    set: ValueSetter | SequenceSetter | None = None,
    size: SizeGetter | None = None,
) -> None

Add a custom configuration entry.

This function extends the root configuration with user-defined entries. Depending on the entry name and callbacks, different types of entries are created. The following examples show typical usage patterns:

  • A group entry (for example, custom) can be added without any callbacks. This groups other entries and does not have a value.

  • A scalar value entry (for example, custom.val) can be added by passing value getter and setter callbacks.

  • A sequence entry (for example, custom.arr[]) can be added by passing a size getter callback. Child entries should then use sequence getter and setter callbacks to access the values of individual elements.

  • A sequence element entry (for example, custom.arr[].val) can be added by passing sequence getter and setter callbacks. The index of the element is passed to the callbacks. The index must be optional and is omitted if the entry is accessed without an index (for example, custom.arr.val). It is up to the user to decide how to handle this case. Possibilities include accessing the first element or a default one.

Apart from the requirement that there is at most one sequence entry on any chain of config entries, callbacks can be freely combined and there is some freedom in how to implement them.

items.text:
profile: list[dict[str, Any]]

Get the profiling information as a list of profile nodes.

Profiling data is only collected if profiling is enabled via the --profile option. Otherwise, the list is empty.

Each node is a dictionary. Internal nodes have the keys "type" ("internal"), "key", "nested", and "children". The key is the string representation of an expression in the logic program, nested indicates whether the node's times are already included in its parent node, and children is the list of child nodes. Leaf nodes have the keys "type" ("leaf"), "profile_type" ("step" for the last step or "accu" for all steps), "matches", "instances", "time_instantiate", and "time_propagate", where the times are given in nanoseconds.

items.title: main
items.text:
main() -> None

Ground and solve a logic program based on the current control mode.

This function serves as a high-level entry point for the default ground-and-solve process. It proceeds as follows:

  1. If a script defines a main function, execution is dispatched to it.
  2. Otherwise, in ControlMode.Parse and ControlMode.Rewrite, the parsed or rewritten program is printed.
  3. Otherwise, if the program includes <incmode>, incremental grounding and solving is performed.
  4. Otherwise, the program parts in parts (or the base part if none are set) are grounded, followed by a single solve call in ControlMode.Solve.

Before calling main(), the control object can be prepared by parsing programs, registering propagators, or performing other setup steps.

items.title: start_solve
items.text:
start_solve(
    assumptions: Sequence[tuple[Symbol, bool] | int] = [],
    on_model: Callable[[Model], bool | None] | None = None,
    on_unsat: Callable[[Sequence[int]], None] | None = None,
    on_stats: Callable[[Stats, Stats], None] | None = None,
    on_finish: Callable[[SolveResult], None] | None = None,
    yield_: bool = False,
    async_: bool = False,
) -> SolveHandle

Start solving the current ground program.

This function runs the solver on the current ground program, optionally using assumptions, callbacks, or asynchronous execution. It returns a SolveHandle, allowing interaction with the solving process.

If asynchronous solving (async_) is enabled, the function returns immediately, and solving runs in the background. Otherwise, if yielding (yield_) is enabled, models are computed one at a time when they are requested via the handle. If neither is enabled, the function blocks until solving is complete.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default assumptions Sequence[tuple[Symbol, bool] | int]

The assumptions that constrain the search. Each assumption is either a tuple[clingo.symbol.Symbol, bool] indicating an atom's truth value or a program literal (see literal). For example, using [(clingo.symbol.Function(lib, "a"), True)] only admits answer sets that contain atom a.

[] on_model Callable[[Model], bool | None] | None

An optional callback that receives a Model object when a model is found. Returning False from the callback stops solving.

None on_unsat Callable[[Sequence[int]], None] | None

An optional callback to intercept lower bounds during optimization.

None on_stats Callable[[Stats, Stats], None] | None

An optional callback that receives statistics updates after each step. Two Stats objects are passed: the step-specific and the accumulated stats.

None on_finish Callable[[SolveResult], None] | None

An optional callback called once the search has finished. A SolveResult is passed to the callback.

None yield_ bool

If True, the returned SolveHandle is iterable, yielding Model objects during solving.

False async_ bool

If True, solving runs asynchronously in a separate thread. Callbacks (on_model, on_stats, etc.) are then also called from a separate thread.

False

Returns:

Type Description SolveHandle

A handle to control the search.

Notes

Asynchronous solving requires compiling clingo with thread support. Blocking methods on SolveHandle release the GIL but are not thread-safe.

See Also

solve

items.title: write_aspif
items.text:
write_aspif(
    path: str | None = None,
    symbols: bool = False,
    append: bool = False,
    preamble: bool | None = None,
    preprocess: bool = True,
) -> None

Write the current logic program in aspif format.

If path is None, the program is written to clingo's internal output buffer, which is available via buffer. Otherwise, it is written to the given file, which is created if it does not exist.

If append is false, an existing file is overwritten. Output to the buffer is always appended to its current content.

If preamble is None, the aspif preamble is written unless the program is appended to existing content, i.e., unless append is true and the file exists or the buffer is non-empty. In application mode, the buffer is printed to stdout and cleared after each major operation like grounding, so the preamble flag should be set explicitly in this case.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str | None

The optional path to write the program to.

None symbols bool

Whether to also write the symbols of the program.

False append bool

Whether to append to existing content.

False preamble bool | None

Whether to write the aspif preamble.

None preprocess bool

Whether to preprocess the program before writing.

True

items.title: clingo.ground
items.text: Functions and classes related to grounding.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The example shows how call external functions during grounding:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.symbol import Number
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>>
>>> class Context:
...     def __init__(self, lib):
...       self.lib = lib
...     def inc(self, x):
...         return Number(self.lib, x.number + 1)
...     def seq(self, x, y):
...         return [x, y]
...
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib)
>>> ctl.parse_string("""
... p(@inc(10)).
... q(@seq(1,2)).
... """)
>>> ctl.ground(context=Context(lib))
>>> print(ctl.solve(on_model=print))
p(11) q(1) q(2)
SAT

The example below shows how to start grounding in the background and wait for grounding to finish:

>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib)
>>> ctl.parse_string("{a}.")
>>> with ctl.start_ground() as hnd:
...     w = {True: "finished", False: "running"}
...     print(f"start_ground status: {w[hnd.wait(0)]}")
...     print(f"start_ground result: {hnd.get()!r}")
...     print(f"start_ground status: {w[hnd.wait(0)]}")
...
start_ground status: running
start_ground result: <GroundResult.Ok: 0>
start_ground status: finished

items.title: clingo.propagate
items.text: Functions and classes to implement custom propagators.

items.title: Example
items.text:
>>> from collections.abc import Sequence
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.propagate import Assignment, PropagateControl, PropagateInit, Propagator
>>> from clingo.symbol import Function
>>>
>>> LIB = Library()
>>>
>>> class AIFFB(Propagator):
...     slit_a: int
...     slit_b: int
...
...     def __init__(self) -> None:
...         super().__init__()
...         self.slit_a = 0
...         self.slit_b = 0
...
...     # add watches for atoms `a` and `b`
...     def init(self, assignment: Assignment, init: PropagateInit) -> None:
...         # get program literals for atoms `a` and `b`
...         plit_a = init.base[Function(LIB, "a")].literal
...         plit_b = init.base[Function(LIB, "b")].literal
...         # get solver literals for program literals `a` and `b`
...         self.slit_a = init.solver_literal(plit_a)
...         self.slit_b = init.solver_literal(plit_b)
...         # add watches for solver literals `a` and `b`
...         init.add_watch(self.slit_a)
...         init.add_watch(self.slit_b)
...
...     # propagate solver literals `a` and `b`
...     def propagate(self, assignment: Assignment, control: PropagateControl, changes: Sequence[int]) -> None:
...         # if `a` is true imply `b`
...         if self.slit_a in changes:
...             assert assignment.is_true(self.slit_a)
...             control.add_clause([-self.slit_a, self.slit_b])
...         # if `b` is true imply `a`
...         if self.slit_b in changes:
...             assert assignment.is_true(self.slit_b)
...             control.add_clause([-self.slit_b, self.slit_a])
...
>>> ctl = Control(LIB, ["0"])
>>> ctl.register_propagator(AIFFB())
>>> ctl.parse_string("1 { a; b }.")
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> print(ctl.solve(on_model=print))
a b
SAT

items.title: Trail
items.text:
Bases: Sequence[int]

Provides access to literals in the solver's trail.

The trail represents the sequence of literals assigned during the solving process. It is structured by decision levels, where each level contains literals assigned due to implications from the decision literal at that level.

The literals within each level are ordered by implication, reflecting the logical dependencies between them as determined by the solver's propagation and learning mechanisms. The decision literal for each level is placed at the beginning of its respective sequence.

This provides a read-only sequence interface to access the solver literals in the trail. The trail is only valid during the propagator callback in which it was obtained.

items.title: Assignment
items.text:
Bases: Sequence[int]

Provides information about the current state of literals in the solver.

It provides methods to inspect and query the assignment, which is essential for implementing custom propagators.

Key concepts:

  • Each literal is either true, false, or unassigned.
  • Each assigned literal has a decision level.
  • There is exactly one decision literal per level.
  • All other literals on the same level are implied by the decision literal and literals from earlier levels.
  • The current decision level is the highest level at which literals are assigned.
  • The root level is the lowest decision level that can be backtracked to.

This provides a read-only sequence interface to access the positive solver literals, i.e., one entry per solver variable, independent of their truth values. The assignment is only valid during the propagator callback in which it was obtained.

Class for controlling propagators.

This class provides methods for adding clauses, literals, and nogoods, as well as managing watches and performing propagation.

items.title: Propagator
items.text:
Propagator()

Interface for implementing propagators.

This class defines methods that can be overridden to create custom propagators for use with the solver.

Only the methods overridden in the class of a propagator are called by the solver. Methods that are not overridden are not registered with the solver at all, which avoids the overhead of calling into Python. This matters, for example, for decide, which is called very often during search. The overridden methods are determined when the propagator is registered; methods assigned to an instance are ignored.

The default implementations, which can be called via super(), do nothing except decide, which returns the fallback literal.

Construct a propagator.

items.title: clingo.script
items.text: Module to add custom scripts that can be embedded into logic programs.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The following example shows how to register a custom python script that executes functions from the main context (just like the embedded one in the standalone clingo).

>>> import __main__
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.script import Script, register
>>> from clingo.symbol import Number, Symbol
...
>>> class PyScript(Script):
...     def execute(self, code) -> None:
...         exec(code, __main__.__dict__, __main__.__dict__)
...     def call(self, lib, name, arguments):
...         return [getattr(__main__, name)(lib, *arguments)]
...     def callable(self, name, arguments) -> bool:
...         return name in __main__.__dict__ and callable(__main__.__dict__[name])
...     def main(self, lib, control) -> None:
...         __main__.main(lib, control)
...     def name(self):
...         return "python"
...     def name(self):
...         return "1.0.0"
...
>>> def f(lib, x):
...     return Number(lib, x.number * 3)
...
>>> lib = Library()
>>> register(lib, PyScript())
>>> ctl = Control(lib, ["--convert=text"])
>>> ctl.parse_string("""\
... #script (python)
...
... from clingo.symbol import Number, Symbol
...
... def g(lib, x):
...     return Number(lib, x.number * 4)
...
... #end.
... p(@f(1)).
... q(@g(2)).
... """)
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> ctl.buffer
"""\
p(3).
q(8).
#show p/1.
#show q/1.
#show.
"""

items.title: clingo.solve
items.text: Functions and classes related to solving.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The examples below show various ways to intercept models. The asynchronous variants leave room for additional computation before calling blocking functions like get or model.

The following example shows how to intercept models with a callback:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib, ["0"])
>>> ctl.parse_string("1 { a; b } 1.")
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> print(ctl.solve(on_model=print))
a
b
SAT

The following example shows how to yield models:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib, ["0"])
>>> ctl.parse_string("1 { a; b } 1.")
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> with ctl.start_solve(yield_=True) as hnd:
...     for mdl in hnd:
...         print(mdl)
...     print(hnd.get())
...
a
b
SAT

The following example shows how to solve asynchronously:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib, ["0"])
>>> ctl.parse_string("1 { a; b } 1.")
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> with ctl.start_solve(on_model=print, async_=True) as hnd:
...     # other work: poll with wait or use on_finish
...     print(hnd.get())
...
a
b
SAT

This example shows how to solve both iteratively and asynchronously:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib, ["0"])
>>> ctl.parse_string("1 { a; b } 1.")
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> with ctl.start_solve(yield_=True, async_=True) as hnd:
...     # other work: poll with wait or use on_finish
...     while mdl := hnd.model():
...         print(mdl)
...         hnd.resume()
...         # other work: poll with wait or use on_finish
...     print(hnd.get())
...
b
a
SAT

An object to interact with a running search.

items.title: clingo.stats
items.text: Functions and classes related to solver stats.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The following example shows how to add custom stats and access the stats:

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>>
>>> def on_stats(step, accu):
...     step.update({"example": [21]})
...     accu.update({"example": [lambda x: (x or 0) + 21]})
...
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib, ['--stats'])
>>> ctl.parse_string("{a}.")
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> print(ctl.solve(on_stats=on_stats))
SAT
>>> print(ctl.solve(on_stats=on_stats))
SAT
>>> ctl.stats['user_step'].nestify()
{ "example": [21.0] }
>>> ctl.stats['user_accu'].nestify()
{ "example": [42.0] }
>>> ctl.stats['summary']['times'].nestify()
{ "cpu": 0.000785999999999995,
  "sat": 7.867813110351562e-06,
  "solve": 2.288818359375e-05,
  "total": 0.0007848739624023438,
  "unsat": 0.0 }

Note that the control object is created passing options --stats; without this option only basic stats are reported.

items.text: Functions and classes for symbol manipulation.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.symbol import Function, Number, parse_term
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>>
>>> num = Number(lib, 42)
>>> num.number
42
>>> fun = Function(lib, "f", [num])
>>> fun.name
'f'
>>> [ str(arg) for arg in fun.arguments ]

items.title: Symbol
items.text:
Represents a clingo symbol.

This includes #inf and #sup, numbers, strings, tuples, functions (including constants with len(arguments) == 0.

Symbol objects implement Python's rich comparison operators and are ordered like in clingo. They can also be used as keys in dictionaries. Their string representation corresponds to their clingo representation.

Note that this class does not have a constructor. Instead there are the preconstructed symbols Infimum and Supremum and the functions Number, String, Tuple_, and Function to construct symbol objects.

items.title: clingo.ast
items.text: This module provides functions to work with Abstract Syntax Trees of logic programs.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
The following example shows how to parse individual statements and add them to a control object.

>>> from clingo.core import Library
>>> from clingo.control import Control
>>> from clingo import ast
>>>
>>> lib = Library()
>>> ctl = Control(lib, ["--convert=text"])
>>> ctl.parse_string("a(1).")
>>> prg = ast.Program(lib)
>>> prg.add(ast.parse_statement(lib, "b(X+1) :- a(X)."))
>>> prg.add(ast.parse_statement(lib, "c(X+1) :- b(X)."))
>>> ctl.join(prg)
>>> ctl.ground()
>>> ctl.buffer
"""
a(1).
b(2).
c(3).
#show.
#show a/1.
#show b/1.
#show c/1.
"""

The next example shows how to visit an AST and collect variables.

from functools import singledispatch

from clingo.core import Library
from clingo import ast
from clingo.ast import terms, theory

@singledispatch
def collect(stm, vars):
    """
    Collect all variables occurring in statements.
    """
    return stm.visit(collect, vars)

@collect.register
def _(var: terms.TermVariable | theory.TheoryTermVariable, vars):
    vars.add(var.name)

lib = Library()
vars = set()

ast.parse_string(
    lib,
    """\
    a(X) :- b(X,Y).
    b(Z).
    """,
    lambda stm: collect(stm, vars),
)

print(vars)

The last example shows how to use a transformer to modify an AST.

from functools import singledispatch

from clingo.core import Library
from clingo import ast
from clingo.ast import terms

@singledispatch
def rename(stm, lib):
    """
    Replaces all occurrences of variable `X` with `Y` in the given statement
    returning a new statement. If no replacement was made, `None` is returned.
    """
    return stm.transform(lib, rename, lib)

@rename.register
def _(var: terms.TermVariable, lib):
    return var.update(lib, name="Y") if var.name == "X" else None

lib = Library()
stms = []

ast.parse_string(
    lib,
    """\
    b(1,1).
    b(2,3).
    a(X) :- b(X,Y).
    """,
    stms.append,
)

for stm in stms:
    print(rename(stm, lib) or stm)

items.title: AST
items.text:
The base class of all AST nodes.

AST nodes are immutable. They can be compared, ordered, hashed, and converted to strings in clingo's input language. The node types are defined in the submodules of this module. Their arguments are available via read-only properties and __match_args__ to support pattern matching. Modified copies of nodes can be created with update and transform.
